seo.title: Karmic tail 6 14 17 compatibility: The Lovers, Temperance, The Star
seo.description: Karmic tail 6 14 17 compatibility: how a couple moves from admiration, through time, to a star of its own — the three cards, the maths and The Little Prince.

title: Karmic tail 6-14-17 in compatibility: a rose, time and stars that laugh
short: The karmic tail 6-14-17 in compatibility is the story of a couple that begins with admiration and has to learn a light that needs no audience. The Lovers stand at the entry, Temperance in the middle, The Star in the main task. Between the first "how beautiful you are" and a star of their own, this couple has not a rule but time. No personal destiny matrix holds such a tail: only two people together can make it.

sections.h2: The riddle of the middle: why 14 and not 5
paragraphs: In a personal matrix the middle of the tail is not chosen: it is the sum of the two ends. If 6-?-17 were someone's personal tail, The Hierophant would stand in the middle: 6 + 17 = 23, and 23 reduces to 5. A teacher, a rule, "how love ought to be done". This couple has Temperance in that place, and it is not a calculation error. Each point of a couple's matrix is the sum of the same points of two personal matrices, so the couple's middle is built from the partners' middles, not from its own ends.

A run of the site's engine through every date shows what this tail is made of. It occurs in roughly one couple in 45 (2.246%) and ranks 14th among the 97 couple tails. Only three combinations of personal tails produce it:
There are three clues in this table.

**First: the plot belongs to the union, not to either person.** Neither partner carries Temperance or The Star in a personal tail, in any combination. The Lovers appear in only a quarter of couples, in the tail 18-6-6. In three couples out of four, neither of the two has any of the three cards: the entry, the middle and the task come to this couple only together.

**Second: The Hierophant has not gone anywhere.** In 73% of these couples it stands in the middle of one partner's personal tail (15-5-8). Added to the other partner's Hermit, it stops being a rule and becomes a measure: 5 + 9 = 14. Our reading: the "this is how it's done" that one of them brings meets the other's quiet, and the rule turns into time.

**Third: The Lovers made of The Devil and The Moon.** In 97% of these couples The Lovers at the entry are the sum of one partner's Devil and the other's Moon. Wen separates The Lovers from The Devil this way: "Key 6 is about one choice. Key 15 is about being led astray." Our reading: this couple's admiration is made from the start of attachment and night-time imagination, and the choice inside it has yet to be made.

sections.h2: The Little Prince as the story of one couple
paragraphs: Antoine de Saint-Exupéry wrote the tale in 1942 in New York and in Asharoken on Long Island, and it came out in 1943 in English and French at once. It is usually read as a parable about friendship and childhood. But inside it is a love story between two very young creatures, the prince and the rose, and it is told in three acts, exactly in the order of the tail 6-14-17.

The first act is the prince's planet: the rose opens at sunrise, they admire each other, misunderstand each other and part. The second is the Earth: a garden of five thousand identical roses, the Fox and his lesson about time. The third is the stars: from the businessman who counts them and locks them in a drawer to stars that know how to laugh.

The roles here are not split by sex. The prince and the rose are not "him" and "her" but two ways of loving, and in every couple with this tail both partners are sometimes one and sometimes the other. The rose — when the wish is to be admired and tenderness hides behind a whim. The prince — when words are taken literally and leaving is easier than guessing what lies behind them.

sections.h2: Entry to the task — The Lovers: "Oh! How beautiful you are!"
paragraphs: The rose prepared her entrance for a long time. Still hidden in "her green chamber", she chose her colours and adjusted her petals one by one: "It was only in the full radiance of her beauty that she wished to appear." She opened "exactly at sunrise" and promptly yawned: "Ah! I am scarcely awake. I beg that you will excuse me. My petals are still all disarranged..." The prince "could not restrain his admiration": "Oh! How beautiful you are!" — "Am I not? And I was born at the same moment as the sun..."

In Lisovskaya's reading, the Entry to the task point is what the couple wants together: shared wishes, agreements, a common language. The point stands on the line of tasks, so the same wish also turns into resistance. For a 6-14-17 couple the wish at the entry is this: to admire and to be admired. Wen writes of The Lovers in questions of love: "the beginnings of romance and, simultaneously, the beginnings of temptation", and at the start "a strong feeling of paradise, at least in the beginning". Such unions are said to be made in heaven. The rose really did come from the sky: she grew "from a seed blown from no one knew where".

The resistance hides in that same language. The rose prepared for days, yet pretends she has only just woken. Then come the tigers that do not live on the planet, the draughts, the screen, and the cough "in order to put the little prince in the wrong". The prince hears every word. "He had taken seriously words which were without importance, and it made him very unhappy." In a couple's life this is recognisable at once. One complains in order to be noticed, and the other answers the complaint instead of the request. One says "go, then, if you've decided" and waits to be stopped, and the other picks up a coat.

The prince only draws the conclusion later, on Earth: **"I ought to have judged by deeds and not by words."** And straight after: "She cast her fragrance and her radiance over me. I ought never to have run away from her... I ought to have guessed all the affection that lay behind her poor little stratagems."

There is no culprit in this scene, and that matters for the whole tail. Saying goodbye, the rose tells him: "Of course I love you. It is my fault that you have not known it all the while. That is of no importance. But you, you have been just as foolish as I." And at once, so that he will not see her tears: "You have decided to go away. Now go!" This was the choice of The Lovers, made in the language of pride. Not "I don't love you" but "I won't show you that it hurts". The task at the entry is not to stop admiring. This couple's admiration is real. The task is to hear the tenderness behind the performance and to stop staging performances.

sections.h2: Middle of the task — Temperance: the time wasted for the rose
paragraphs: On Earth the prince finds a garden where five thousand roses bloom, exactly like his. "I thought that I was rich, with a flower that was unique in all the world; and all I had was a common rose." He lies down in the grass and cries. This is how this couple's chief enemy enters the story — comparison. But the answer to it comes not from The Star but from the middle of the road: the Fox.

The Fox explains that taming means "to establish ties" and teaches how it is done: "You must be very patient. First you will sit down at a little distance from me, like that, in the grass... you will say nothing. Words are the source of misunderstandings. But you will sit a little closer to me, every day..." This is a direct answer to the entry to the task. The common language of The Lovers is words, and it failed. Temperance offers not new words but a distance that shrinks by one blade of grass a day.

Then the Fox talks about the hour: **"If, for example, you come at four o'clock in the afternoon, then at three o'clock I shall begin to be happy."** And about rites: they "are what make one day different from other days, one hour from other hours". The hunters have their Thursday, when they dance with the village girls, and that day is wonderful. Wen recalls that twentieth-century writers called Temperance the Time card. The Fox describes time exactly so: the coming hour pours into the present one, and happiness begins an hour before the meeting.

And now the key clue of the whole article. In parting, the Fox tells the prince his secret. In the French original it runs: "C'est le temps que tu as perdu pour ta rose qui fait ta rose si importante." Katherine Woods, in the first English translation of 1943: "It is the time you have wasted for your rose that makes your rose so important." Andrei Sharov's Russian version: "because you gave her all your time" (our translation). And Nora Gal's canonical Russian translation, the one through which almost every Russian reader knows the tale (our translation):
**"Your rose is so dear to you because you gave her your whole soul."**

Time has turned into soul. Nora Gal does this twice. In the original, the switchman's children lose time over a rag doll: Woods has "They waste their time over a rag doll", Sharov "they don't begrudge the time they spend fussing over a rag doll". In Nora Gal they "give their whole soul to a rag doll". It is a beautiful translation, but for a 6-14-17 couple the difference is real. A soul can be given in a single rush, at dawn, at the sight of a beauty: that is The Lovers. Time cannot be given that way, only an hour at a time, and that is Temperance. The word itself matters too: in Saint-Exupéry, time is not "invested" but "lost", wasted. The Fox praises not an investment but a spending without calculation.

Right after the Fox the book sets his opposite — a merchant selling pills that quench thirst. "Because they save a tremendous amount of time... With these pills, you save fifty-three minutes in every week." The prince thinks: **"If I had fifty-three minutes to spend as I liked, I should walk at my leisure toward a spring of fresh water."** Among Waite's divinatory meanings for Temperance the first is economy. This couple's middle teaches the opposite: to save time for each other, not at each other's expense.

At its worst, Temperance in Lisovskaya is one partner always giving way while the other never even notices. It is haste, and a feeling that nobody knows what the relationship is for. In the tale, haste is shown by the switchman: express trains thunder past in both directions, and "not even the locomotive engineer knows" what the passengers are looking for. "No one is ever satisfied where he is," he says in Woods; Nora Gal gives him the Russian proverb "Tam khorosho, gde nas net" — "it is good wherever we are not". Waite writes that under the rule of Temperance we know "something of whence we came and whither we are going". A couple in the shadow of the middle rides an express without knowing where to. A couple at its best knows its own four o'clock.

And one more detail that is easy to miss: who tamed whom? The prince tells the Fox: "There is a flower... I think that she has tamed me..." The ties of this middle run both ways. When the prince goes back to the five thousand roses, he lists what sets his rose apart from them. Nothing but the time they lived through: "because it is she that I have watered... because it is she that I have listened to, when she grumbled, or boasted, or even sometimes when she said nothing. Because she is my rose." What defeats comparison with others is not being different, but this list.

sections.h2: Main task — The Star: stars in a drawer and stars that laugh
paragraphs: The Main task point is read mostly through its shadow side: what the couple fails at and what it has to learn. At its worst, The Star in Lisovskaya is a beautiful wrapping with nothing inside and a union put on display. It is comparison with others and pride in status, when one partner belittles the other. It is treating the partner as a fan. It is fear of fulfilling one's own dream and a habit of getting in the way of the partner's. And it is being in love without responsibility. The prince's journey across the planets reads as a gallery of these shadows.

On the second planet lives a conceited man. "Ah! Ah! I am about to receive a visit from an admirer!" he cries when he sees the prince from afar: "For, to conceited men, all other men are admirers." He asks for applause, raises his hat and explains that to admire means to regard him as "the handsomest, the best-dressed, the richest, and the most intelligent man on this planet". — "But you are the only man on your planet!" A couple in the shadow of The Star recognises itself here easily. One partner expects applause from the other on demand and takes offence when it is too faint. Or both expect it from an audience and live for the photograph.

The businessman counts the stars: "Five-hundred-and-one million, six-hundred-twenty-two thousand, seven-hundred-thirty-one. I am concerned with matters of consequence: I am accurate." He owns them: he writes the number on a little paper and locks it in a drawer. The prince answers him with a line that could serve as the formula of the main task: "I myself own a flower, which I water every day... It is of some use to my volcanoes, and it is of some use to my flower, that I own them. But you are of no use to the stars..." Another person's light can be counted as property and kept in a drawer. Or it can be watered.

The lamplighter is the only one the prince does not find ridiculous: "When he lights his street lamp, it is as if he brought one more star to life, or one flower." His trouble is his orders — in Nora Gal, his "agreement": once he put the lamp out in the morning and lit it in the evening, but now "from year to year the planet has turned more rapidly and the orders have not been changed!" This speaks directly to the Entry to the task point, where the couple's shared agreements live. The agreement of the first days works while the planet turns slowly. When life speeds up and the agreement stays the same, the light goes on and off every minute and there is not a second left for rest.

The prince answers the whole gallery on his last night: **"Where I live everything is so small that I cannot show you where my star is to be found. It is better, like that. My star will just be one of the stars, for you."** This couple's star is not the one that gets displayed. "All men have the stars, but they are not the same things for different people. For some, who are travellers, the stars are guides. For others they are no more than little lights in the sky. For others, who are scholars, they are problems. For my businessman they were wealth. But all these stars are silent." For the one who loved, though, the stars will laugh. His friends will be astonished to see him laughing at the sky and will think he is crazy. A light that only two people understand looks strange from outside, and that is what makes it real.

Even a number changes its meaning here. The businessman locked half a billion stars in a drawer — as a number on a little paper. At the end the prince gives the pilot the same number, only alive: "You will have five hundred million little bells, and I shall have five hundred million springs of fresh water..." For him the stars are now "wells with a rusty pulley. All the stars will pour out fresh water for me to drink..."

The Fox has one last lesson too: **"You become responsible, forever, for what you have tamed. You are responsible for your rose..."** In Lisovskaya, The Star at its worst is a couple that enjoys being in love until the question of responsibility comes up. The Fox answers before the question is asked: admiration lived through time becomes responsibility.

The whole tail fits into one sentence about the water from the well that the pilot and the prince reached at daybreak. **"This water was indeed a different thing from ordinary nourishment. Its sweetness was born of the walk under the stars, the song of the pulley, the effort of my arms."** The long walk is Temperance. Under the stars is The Star. And it was sought for one thing only: "what they are looking for could be found in one single rose, or in a little water."

sections.h2: What Waite's cards show: noon, two cups and the stars
paragraphs: These are the drawings of the Waite–Smith deck; the cards on this site are drawn differently. But in Waite the three cards of the tail add up to a single day, from the noon sun to the stars.

On The Lovers "the sun shines in the zenith", and beneath it is a winged figure with arms extended. Waite calls it "in all simplicity the card of human love", love before it is contaminated by "gross material desire". The rose, remember, "was born at the same moment as the sun".

On Temperance the angel has "the sign of the sun upon his forehead". He pours liquid from chalice to chalice, and "a direct path goes up to certain heights on the verge of the horizon", above which shines a great light. Waite adds: "I speak of him in the masculine sense, but the figure is neither male nor female." For the middle of a couple's tail this is a precise hint: the work of time is not divided into "his" and "hers". Wen quotes P. D. Ouspensky's The Symbolism of the Tarot: "The name of the angel is Time... One of the cups the angel holds is the past, the other is the future. The rainbow stream between the cups is the present. You see that it flows both ways." The Fox at four o'clock, happy from three, is that same stream.

On The Star the sun is gone: a great star of eight rays and seven lesser ones shine, and a woman pours water from two great ewers onto the land and into the pool. Wen compares her with Temperance: there, a balancing; here, "a pouring out in one direction". The middle of the tail is an exchange; the main task is a light that pours out without expecting a return. Waite adds that on other planes the card "has been certified as immortality and interior light". The tale describes that interior light exactly: the pilot carries the sleeping prince and sees in him "the image of a rose that shines through his whole being like the flame of a lamp, even when he is asleep".

And a small thing that proves nothing but raises a smile. Waite notes that in some later cards the bird on The Star's tree was replaced by "a butterfly on a rose". And the rose, saying goodbye to the prince, tells him: "Well, I must endure the presence of two or three caterpillars if I wish to become acquainted with the butterflies."

sections.h2: The rose who had a voice of her own
paragraphs: The rose had a real model, and her story adds the tail's last clue. Consuelo Suncín was born in 1901 in El Salvador; she wrote, painted and sculpted. She and Antoine de Saint-Exupéry met at the end of 1930 in Buenos Aires and married in the spring of 1931. The marriage was stormy: he left and came back many times. Consuelo had asthma, and the rose in the tale coughs. Biographers see her as the model for the capricious, vain and fragile flower. In 1942, while the tale was being written, they lived at Bevin House on Long Island.

On 31 July 1944 Saint-Exupéry did not return from a reconnaissance flight. Consuelo wrote a memoir of the marriage, and the manuscript lay in a trunk for a long time. Mémoires de la rose (in English, The Tale of the Rose) came out only in 2000 and was translated into many languages. Earlier still, in 1945, her book Oppède appeared in New York with her own drawings.

This is not a model for a couple and not a forecast. It is a detail that clarifies the main task. The rose in the tale speaks in hints, tigers and coughs. The living woman behind that rose told the story herself, in her own voice. The Star in the tail 6-14-17 is not a role played in someone else's light, but each partner's own light.

sections.h2: How this tail's circle closes and where it opens
paragraphs: Put the three acts together and a circle appears, one that a couple with this tail can walk for years without noticing it is a circle:

ol: **A performance of admiration.** One shows themselves in the best light and waits for delight; the other admires. Both are in paradise, like the rose and the prince at sunrise.
**Words instead of deeds.** Requests come out as complaints, tenderness hides behind barbs. The other hears the words literally, feels guilty and leaves — the room, for work, into silence.
**Time on the run.** Meeting "when we can", life on an express train, fifty-three minutes saved at each other's expense. One keeps adjusting, the other does not see it.

**Five thousand roses.** The couple starts comparing itself with other couples, and the partner with other people. Someone lies down in the grass and cries: "that doesn't make me a very great prince". Someone chooses the shop window and looks for admiration from an audience.
**Hunger for admiration again.** The less time and truth there is, the stronger the wish for someone to applaud. The circle returns to the first step.

paragraphs: It opens at every step with a move of its own, and every one of these moves is in the tale:

ul: **Judge by deeds.** Hear a request in a complaint, and "it hurts" in "now go".
**Keep a four o'clock of their own.** A time that repeats and is never moved: a Thursday, an evening, a ritual that belongs to the two of them.
**Waste time together.** Do not economise on those fifty-three minutes: the middle of the road grows out of them.
**Revise the lamplighter's orders.** Check the agreements of the first days against how the planet turns now.
**Do not count the other's stars.** Support the other's dream instead of owning it and locking it in a drawer.
**Answer for what has been tamed.** When admiration quietens down, the thing the whole road was for begins.

paragraphs: If threats, pressure or fear for personal safety have entered the relationship, that is no longer a matter for the tail. Then it is worth seeing a psychologist, and in danger, calling a local emergency number.

sections.h2: The strong version of the tail 6-14-17
paragraphs: At its best, The Star in Lisovskaya is a union that inspires both. The partners say plainly what they like and what they don't, and often it is only as a couple that they understand who they want to be. It is the rare case where the pretty picture is true. A 6-14-17 couple has beauty from the very entry, and the main task is not to give it up. The task is for the picture to stop being a performance.

The tale has this version too. At six, the pilot gave up drawing because grown-ups did not understand his boa constrictors. Beside the prince he draws again — a sheep, a box, a muzzle — and in the end illustrates the book himself. The prince asks nothing of his drawings; he only laughs that the baobabs "look a little like cabbages" and reassures him: "children understand." The Star at its best is when, beside another person, someone dares to take up what they once abandoned.

The two dates that give the couple tail 6-14-17 were calculated by the site's engine. The first partner's personal tail is 15-5-8, the second's 18-9-9 — the most common combination, 73% of such couples.

The couple's values for these dates are 12, The Hanged Man. The Star stands here twice, and that is not a doubling but two different roles. In the main task it is read through its shadow side, as a lesson: the shop window, comparisons, another's light in a drawer. On the What to create together point, which is read only at its best, it is what the couple is meant to create: a light of its own that inspires both.

The check of the middle on these dates is plain to see. By the personal formula, 6 + 17 would give 5. In the couple the middle is the sum of the partners' middles: 5 + 9 = 14. The first partner's Hierophant is literally visible in the sum, and together with the second partner's Hermit it turns into Temperance.

sections.h2: The Tower at the centre and the couple's values
paragraphs: In 97.5% of couples with this tail the centre holds 16, The Tower; in the remaining 2.5%, 7, The Chariot. In Lisovskaya the couple's centre is the atmosphere inside the union, what is not on show. The Tower at its best means trials passed hand in hand, calm in sudden trouble, often an unusual story of how they met. At its worst, barbs and threats of a break-up used as leverage. Wen observes that The Star comes straight after The Tower in the deck: "After the downfall of The Tower, The Star is an indication of a turn upward." The tale begins the same way — with a forced landing in the desert: "Something was broken in my engine." The stars appear in it only after the crash. Saint-Exupéry had such a crash himself: in 1935 he came down in the Libyan Desert and, with his mechanic, wandered for four days without water until a Bedouin gave them a drink. He told the story in Terre des hommes, whose English title is Wind, Sand and Stars.

There is an arithmetic detail as well. In a personal matrix the entry of the tail equals the sum of the main task and the centre. For this couple the formula holds with both possible centres: 17 + 16 = 33 → 6 and 17 + 7 = 24 → 6. The admiration at the entry is literally made of a star and a crash.

The couple's values (spiritual purpose) in such couples are 21, The World (49.3%), 3, The Empress (27.1%), and 12, The Hanged Man (23.7%). What follows is our reading through the tale. The World is the journey across the planets that leads back home to the rose. The Empress is the garden and the care of a living thing, that same watering every morning. The Hanged Man is the ability to look at the same sky differently: "all men have the stars, but they are not the same things for different people".

ul: **Entry to the task — 6, The Lovers.** The couple enters its task through delight and beauty: it wants to love and be loved the way it did on the first day. Its common language is the language of admiration, hints and little performances, and that same language is the first thing to get in the way of understanding.

**Middle of the task — 14, Temperance.** The road runs through measure and time: drawing closer little by little, keeping an hour that belongs to the two of them, never saving time at each other's expense.

**Main task — 17, The Star.** Learning a light that does not need to be put on show: each becoming themselves beside the other and not dimming the other's dream. At its worst: a shop window, comparisons, and a partner cast as a fan.

intro: This plot was written down long ago, and almost everyone read it as a child. In Saint-Exupéry's The Little Prince, the story of the prince and the rose runs exactly in the order of the tail: a beauty at sunrise, the Fox and his lesson about time, stars that know how to laugh. The key to the middle is hidden in a single line of the Fox's — and the classic Russian translation gives it in a different form from the one the author wrote.

faq.q: What does the karmic tail 6-14-17 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is the task of a couple that enters a relationship through admiration and beauty (6, The Lovers), lives it through time, measure and patience (14, Temperance) and learns a light that needs no audience (17, The Star). The main task is read through its shadow side: a shop window, comparison with others, a partner cast as a fan, fear of fulfilling one's own dream and of getting in the way of the other's.

faq.q: Why is the middle of the tail 14 if 6 + 17 gives 5?
faq.a: In a personal matrix the middle is built from the ends of the tail, while in a couple's matrix each point is the sum of the same points of two personal matrices. The couple's middle 14 comes from the partners' middles: 5 + 9, 8 + 6 or 10 + 4. That is why the tail 6-14-17 never occurs in one person's personal chart.

faq.q: Are there couple tails made of the same numbers?
faq.a: No. The entry of a couple's tail can only be 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18 or 21, so 14 and 17 cannot stand there, and the order 6-17-14 does not arise from any two dates. 6-14-17 is the only couple tail made of these three numbers.

faq.q: Is this a bad tail? Does it mean the couple will break up?
faq.a: No. The tail does not predict events or pass verdicts: it describes a task, not an outcome. This couple's task is to learn to judge by deeds, to give the relationship time and not to confuse an audience's admiration with a light of its own.

faq.q: How common is the karmic tail 6-14-17?
faq.a: It occurs in roughly one couple in 45, which is 2.246% of all couples and 14th place among the 97 couple tails. It is made of three combinations of personal tails: 15-5-8 and 18-9-9 (73%), 15-8-11 and 18-6-6 (24%), 21-10-7 and 21-4-10 (2%).

report: One of the best-known lines in The Little Prince reaches Russian readers in a different form from the one Saint-Exupéry wrote. In the French original the Fox speaks of time lost, and Katherine Woods' English keeps it: "It is the time you have wasted for your rose that makes your rose so important." Nora Gal's canonical Russian translation reads (our translation): **"Your rose is so dear to you because you gave her your whole soul."** For a couple with the tail 6-14-17, that difference is the whole plot.

The tail reads as the three acts of that tale. At the entry to the task stand The Lovers: the couple comes in through admiration and beauty. In the middle, Temperance: the road runs through measure and time. In the main task, The Star: a light that needs no audience. In one person's personal chart The Hierophant would stand between The Lovers and The Star — a rule, "how love ought to be done". This couple has time in that place, and only two people together can make it.

report.h3: The star that cannot be shown

report: The main task is read through its shadow side, and the prince's journey across the planets is a gallery of that shadow. The conceited man cries "Ah! Ah! I am about to receive a visit from an admirer!" and asks for applause, though there is nobody else on his planet. That is the partner cast as a fan, and applause on demand. The businessman counts the stars, writes the number on a little paper and locks it in a drawer. The prince answers him: "it is of some use to my flower, that I own them. But you are of no use to the stars..." Another's light can be kept in a drawer like property, or it can be watered.

The lamplighter lights his lamp, and "it is as if he brought one more star to life, or one flower". But his orders never change, though "from year to year the planet has turned more rapidly". The agreements of the first days work while the planet turns slowly.

The prince gives the answer on his last night: his star is too small to point out, and **"It is better, like that."** For everyone else the stars are silent, but for the one who loved they will laugh, and friends will think he is crazy. A light that only two people understand looks strange from outside, and that is what makes it real. The businessman locked half a billion stars in a drawer; the prince gives the same number away alive, as "five hundred million little bells" and "five hundred million springs of fresh water". The Fox's last lesson is about this too: "You are responsible for your rose..." Admiration lived through time becomes responsibility.

report.h3: Water born of the walk under the stars

report: The whole tail fits into one sentence about the water from the well that the pilot and the prince reached at daybreak: **"Its sweetness was born of the walk under the stars, the song of the pulley, the effort of my arms."** The long walk is Temperance, the stars are The Star, and it was sought for one thing only: "what they are looking for could be found in one single rose, or in a little water."
The circle of this tail opens with the same moves as in the tale:

ul: judge by deeds, and hear "it hurts" in "now go";
keep a four o'clock of the couple's own that is never moved;
waste time together instead of saving it at each other's expense;
check the agreements of the first days against how the planet turns now;
support the other's dream instead of locking it in a drawer.

report: The rose had a living model, Consuelo de Saint-Exupéry. In the tale the rose speaks in hints and coughs, but the living woman told the story of the marriage herself, in her own voice, in a book of her own. The Star in this tail is not a role played in someone else's light, but each partner's own light.

If threats, pressure or fear for personal safety have entered the relationship, that is no longer a matter for the tail: it is worth seeing a psychologist, and in danger, calling a local emergency number or crisis line.

unit.title: Time wasted for the rose

captions.M: To want admiration and to speak in hints
captions.N: To draw closer hour by hour, not save time on each other
captions.D: To shine without an audience, not lock up the other's dream

unit.meaning: Your task is to move from admiration, through time, to a light that needs no audience, and to guard each other's dreams.
